title: Only reform
hook: Shu'ayb says: I want only reform, as far as I am able, and my success is from Allah (11:88)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guests and Lut, two hosts who guarded strangers. Your line was hospitality protects. Who did you greet, and what did you offer? Day four hundred thirty-eight.

Open a Muslim graduate's thesis to its first page, or look above the desk in a small family shop, and there's a good chance you'll find a short line of Arabic: wa ma tawfiqi illa billah. My success comes only from God. Most people who write it there know it's from the Qur'an. Fewer know who said it first, or what kind of day he was having. It was Shu'ayb, the prophet of Madyan, the town with the crooked scales you met in al-A'raf. He was being mocked. And the line was half of his answer.

Madyan had sneered: Shu'ayb, does your prayer tell you how we should spend our own money? His answer in verse eighty-eight has three parts. First, in paraphrase: I don't want to go behind your backs and do the very thing I'm forbidding you. No hidden deal, no double standard. Second, in Pickthall's translation: "I desire naught save reform so far as I am able." And third: my success comes only from God; in Him I trust, and to Him I turn. The key word is islah. Its root, s-l-h, means to be sound, whole, working the way it should. The prophet Salih, two days ago, carries the same root in his name. The root also gives sulh, reconciliation, making peace between two people. So islah is repair: of a scale, a market, a friendship. Notice what Shu'ayb doesn't claim. Not: I'll fix everything. As far as I am able. And the results aren't his to own. Then Surah Hud keeps going, past where most people stop quoting. Verse eighty-nine: don't let your quarrel with me push you into wrong. Verse ninety: ask forgiveness; my Lord is merciful, loving, wadud. And their answer, verse ninety-one: we don't understand much of what you say, and if it weren't for your clan, we'd have stoned you. Shu'ayb replies: is my clan more honored by you than God? Even with threats on the table, the reformer stays honest, modest about his reach, and points past himself.
screen: `NOT BEHIND YOUR BACKS.` · `ONLY REFORM, AS FAR AS I'M ABLE.` · `S-L-H — SOUND, WHOLE, AT PEACE.` · `MY LORD IS MERCIFUL, LOVING.` · then, large: `ONLY TO SET THINGS RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fix one small thing. Sit, and breathe. Think of one small thing in your world that isn't quite right: a wobbly chair, a bill that's wrong in your favor, a cold silence between two people you know. Not the whole world. One thing, as far as you're able. Then check Shu'ayb's first rule: is there anything you ask of others that you don't do yourself? Picture setting one thing right. If you pray, you can say his words: my success comes only from God. The bell holds the time.
Islah. Reform, repair, setting things right, from the root s-l-h, to be sound and whole. Shu'ayb wanted only islah, as far as he was able. Today's word.
Your line: only to set things right. Today, fix the one small thing you pictured, and don't tell anyone you did it. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Muslims write or say wa ma tawfiqi illa billah, my success comes only from God, from 11:88, at the start of a book, a thesis or a new venture, and scholars cite Shu'ayb's words as a model for anyone working for reform.

original.note: Arabic: reform, repair, making right; from the root s-l-h, to be sound.

trapdoor: what you thought: reform means big changes from the top.
what it means: setting things right, as far as you're able, with no double standard, and leaving the results to God.
what a scholar hears: in 11:88 islah is paired with tawfiq, success granted by God; the root s-l-h also gives salih, sulh and maslaha, the public good in Islamic law.
